blocks.prompt: Read this out loud
blocks.text: Look up. That is a wind turbine. It is very tall. It has three long white blades. When the wind blows, the blades go around. Around and around. The blades never fly away. They hold on tight to the tall tower. All that turning makes electricity. The electricity runs down the tower and into a wire. The wire goes to your house. So the wind helps your lamp light up at night.

blocks.prompt: The Machine That Catches the Wind
blocks.text: A wind turbine looks like a giant white pinwheel on a pole. It has three blades. One blade is longer than a school bus. When the wind rushes past the blades, they begin to turn. The blades turn a shaft inside the box at the top of the tower. The shaft turns a machine called a generator. The generator makes electricity. The electricity runs down the tower and along wires to houses and schools and shops. A turbine burns nothing. It makes no smoke. It only waits for the wind. On a still day the blades hang quiet, and the turbine makes nothing at all.

blocks.prompt: Why the Blades Are Not Sails
blocks.text: From far away, a wind turbine looks lazy. The blades swing around slowly, maybe fifteen times a minute. But watch the very tip of one blade. The blade is so long that its tip has a huge circle to travel, and it must travel that circle in the same few seconds. On a large turbine the tip can move faster than a race car, over 180 miles per hour. The blades are not sails. A sail gets pushed. A turbine blade gets pulled. Each blade is shaped like an airplane wing, curved on one side and flatter on the other. As the blade slices through the air, it bends that air around itself. The air hurrying over the curved side speeds up and presses less hard. The air on the flatter side presses harder. That difference in pressure lifts the blade sideways, and the sideways lift is what pulls the blade around its circle. Behind the blades sits a long box called the nacelle. Inside it, a spinning shaft turns a generator, and the generator makes electricity. On the roof of the nacelle stands a little wind vane. When the wind swings to a new direction, the vane notices, and motors turn the whole nacelle until the blades face straight into the wind again.

4.title: The Machine That Catches the Wind
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

meta.templateLabel: The Machine That Catches the Wind

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Double the wind speed, get about 8 times the power
Double the blade length, catch 4 times the air
The longest blades pass 100 meters
Albert Betz found the limit in 1919
No turbine can take more than about 59 percent

blocks.prompt: Height Is Everything
blocks.text: Wind turbines are built tall for a reason that has nothing to do with looking impressive. Down near the ground, wind drags against hills, trees, fences, and rooftops. That friction slows the air and chops it into gusts. Climb higher and the same wind runs faster and smoother. A turbine on a 300 foot tower reaches better wind than the same machine on a short one, which is why the towers keep growing. The reward for height is bigger than it sounds, because wind power does not add up in a straight line. Double the wind speed and you do not get double the power. You get about eight times as much. The energy in moving air rises with the cube of its speed, so a small gain in wind is worth an enormous gain in electricity. A site with wind averaging 16 miles per hour is not a little better than a site averaging 8. It is worth roughly eight of them. Blade length is lopsided in the same way. The blades sweep out a circle, and doubling the blade length makes that circle four times larger. Four times the circle means four times the air caught. This is why engineers keep stretching blades until the factory, the road, and the crane give up. The longest blades built so far pass 100 meters, longer than a soccer field, and they have to travel in pieces or go by ship. There is a ceiling, though. A turbine can never take all the energy out of the wind, because if it did, the air would stop dead behind the blades and no new air could get through the circle. In 1919 a German physicist named Albert Betz worked out exactly where the limit sits: the most any wind machine can capture is about 59 percent. Good turbines today reach between 35 and 45 percent, which is remarkably close to the theoretical best.

blocks.prompt: The Ohio Basement That Started It
blocks.text: In the winter of 1888, a Cleveland inventor named Charles Brush switched on a machine in his backyard that had never existed before. It was a windmill that made electricity. Windmills themselves were ancient. Persians were grinding grain with the wind more than a thousand years earlier, and Dutch mills had been pumping water out of the lowlands for centuries. But every one of those machines turned wind into motion. Brush's machine turned wind into current. It was a monster by the standards of its day and a curiosity by ours. The wheel measured 56 feet across and carried 144 blades cut from cedar. The whole thing weighed 80,000 pounds. All that machinery produced 12 kilowatts, roughly enough to run a hair dryer and a toaster. Brush stored it in 408 batteries in his basement and lit his house with it for twenty years. The odd part is the blade count. Brush assumed that more blades would catch more wind, and it is an easy thing to assume. A Danish schoolteacher named Poul la Cour proved otherwise. Working in the 1890s with a wind tunnel he built himself, la Cour found that a wheel with few blades, turning fast, beat a wheel crowded with blades, turning slow. Crowded blades spend their time fighting through the churned up air of the blade in front of them. That finding is why the turbine outside your window has three. Three sits at a careful balance point. Two blades are cheaper, but they wobble: when one blade points up into fast wind while the other points down into slow wind, the whole machine strains and shakes. Three blades keep the load even and the tower steady. More than three adds weight and cost without adding much catch. Modern turbines are also fussy about when they work at all. Below about 7 miles per hour there is not enough push to be worth starting. Above about 55, the machine pitches its blades edge on to the wind and deliberately stops itself before something breaks. So a turbine standing still on a wild day is usually not broken. It is being careful.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Betz limit, 1919: about 59 percent is the hard ceiling
Real turbines reach 35 to 45 percent
The slowed air behind a turbine is called the wake
Blades are fiberglass and balsa bonded with resin
Painting one blade black cut bird deaths about 70 percent on Smola
Power scales with the cube of wind speed

blocks.prompt: What the Wind Costs
blocks.text: Every energy source asks for something in return, and the interesting question about wind is not whether it is free. It is what it actually asks for. Start with what the machine is doing. Wind is air with momentum, and a turbine is a device for stealing some of it. The blades are wings, not sails. Air flowing past a blade's curved face speeds up and presses less hard than the air on its flatter face, and that imbalance lifts the blade sideways, hauling it around its circle. A shaft carries the rotation into a generator, and the generator hands the grid a current. Behind the machine, the air leaves slower and messier than it arrived. That slowed, tumbling column is called the wake, and it is why turbines on a wind farm are planted far apart. A turbine standing in another turbine's wake is a turbine being fed leftovers. The physics sets hard walls. Albert Betz showed in 1919 that no wind machine, however clever, can extract more than about 59 percent of the energy in the air passing through it. Taking all of it would mean stopping the air completely, and stopped air plugs the very hole it was flowing through. Real turbines reach 35 to 45 percent. That is not a failure of engineering. It is engineering pressed close to a law. The economics push in exactly one direction: bigger. Power grows with the cube of wind speed, so a taller tower reaching faster, smoother air pays back extravagantly. Power grows with the square of blade length, because a blade twice as long sweeps a circle four times as wide. Both pressures point the same way, which is why the largest turbines now carry blades longer than a soccer field and stand taller than anything else for miles. Now the bill. Those blades are built from fiberglass and balsa wood bonded with resin into a single piece, because a blade that flexes millions of times cannot afford seams that might peel. That same choice makes a blade stubborn to take apart at the end of its life. Steel towers and copper wiring get recycled as a matter of routine. Blades do not. A share of retired ones have been buried in landfills or sawn into bike shelters and footbridges, which is a clever answer at small scale and no answer at all at large scale. Manufacturers are now designing resins that can be chemically undone, which tells you the industry treats this as a real problem rather than a talking point. Birds are the other bill, and the numbers deserve honesty in both directions. Turbines kill birds. So do house cats, windows, cars, and the warming climate that burning fuel accelerates, all by far larger margins. The useful response is not to argue about the ranking. It is to test fixes. On the Norwegian island of Smola, researchers painted one blade of each turbine black, reasoning that three identical blades blur into an invisible smear at speed while a single dark blade breaks the pattern a bird's eye is trying to read. Collisions fell by roughly seventy percent. It cost a bucket of paint. That is the honest shape of wind power. It is not free and it is not magic. It is a very old idea rebuilt with better math, fenced in by a limit from 1919, and still handing us problems worth the trouble of solving.
